name: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections

lead: PRP is made by spinning your own blood to concentrate platelets, then injecting or applying it. In aesthetics it is used for fresher skin, fewer fine lines, brighter under-eyes and hair, and is often paired with microneedling as the 'vampire facial'. Under-eye hollows and dark circles are a common focus, often compared with hyaluronic acid tear-trough filler.

Platelets contain growth factors and cytokines thought to promote tissue repair, which is how treated skin is expected to look fresher. Most controlled trials are on knee osteoarthritis and other joint problems with mixed results, and facial studies are small case series.

paras: A blood draw is centrifuged in a clinic, and the plasma is injected with fine needles or mesotherapy devices, or applied after microneedling, usually as a short series of sessions. It is used on the face, under-eyes and scalp.

Adverse effects are low in most trials, but the CDC linked three HIV diagnoses in 2024 to an unlicensed spa reusing contaminated equipment for vampire facials. PRP itself is not FDA-regulated, so clinical use is off-label, while the preparation devices need clearance.

angle.text: PRP uses your own concentrated platelets, injected or applied with microneedling, for fresher skin, fewer fine lines and brighter under-eyes. The platelets' growth factors are thought to support tissue repair. Trial evidence is mostly from knee osteoarthritis rather than faces.

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma prepared from a person's own blood. The blood is centrifuged to remove red cells while retaining platelets, which contain growth factors and cytokines thought to aid tissue healing. [1] The concentrate is then injected or applied to the target area. In aesthetic medicine it is marketed for wrinkles, skin rejuvenation and hair growth, and it is sometimes combined with microneedling in what is popularly called a 'vampire facial'. [1]

In looksmaxxing forums, PRP is discussed mainly for under-eye hollows and dark circles, often compared with hyaluronic acid tear-trough filler. [2] Most of the clinical research on PRP concerns knee osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal conditions rather than facial appearance, with mixed results. [1][3][4]
The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off-label, while the devices used to prepare it need clearance. [1]
infobox: Centrifugation of the patient's own blood
PRP not regulated as a product; preparation devices FDA-cleared; use off-label

paras: Wikipedia reports that preparation is usually done in a clinic with commercial kits, that protocols aim for roughly three to five times the physiological platelet concentration, and that results vary between individuals and facilities. Platelets may be activated with thrombin or calcium chloride, though this step is optional. [1] Studies have compared single- and double-spin preparation approaches and the effect of leukocyte concentration on knee osteoarthritis outcomes. [5][6]

According to Wikipedia, PRP has been used or studied for tendon and joint problems, hair loss (androgenetic alopecia and alopecia areata), chronic wounds, assisted reproduction, and aesthetic medicine. [1] Registered studies listed for PRP include vocal fold atrophy, rotator cuff conditions, disc disruption and chronic wounds. [7][8][9][10]
In aesthetic practice PRP is applied to the face by injection, with microneedling, or through mesotherapy devices. [1]

Most large human studies concern knee osteoarthritis. Several trials and meta-analyses compared PRP with hyaluronic acid injections. A 2021 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined the comparison [3], while a 2015 randomized trial reported no superiority of PRP over viscosupplementation [11]. A 2017 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial reported that multiple PRP injections performed better than single injections and hyaluronic acid in early osteoarthritis. [12] The 2021 RESTORE randomized trial published in JAMA compared PRP with placebo injection for pain and medial tibial cartilage volume in knee osteoarthritis. [4] A 2017 meta-analysis of randomized trials also examined efficacy. [13]
Wikipedia summarises the overall musculoskeletal picture as mixed: support for some conditions and none for others, with a Cochrane review finding no good evidence for elbow tendinitis. [1]

For facial appearance, the sources reviewed include a 2026 case series that used high-frequency ultrasound to assess PRP injection for facial photoaging  and a 2021 report of seven patients with corticosteroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis treated with PRP mesotherapy. These are small uncontrolled series. No randomized trial of PRP for under-eye appearance was identified in the sources consulted.

Wikipedia reports that adverse effects are low in most trials. [1] In April 2024 the US CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among patients of an unlicensed Albuquerque spa where contaminated single-use equipment was reused in vampire-facial-type procedures. [1]

The introduction to the 2021 RESTORE trial notes that most clinical guidelines at that time did not recommend PRP for knee osteoarthritis because of lack of high-quality evidence, even as use was increasing. [4]
